Q: What is the public SSE contract, and why should the browser not parse raw ADK internals?
A: The API maps runtime events into text_delta, tool_call, tool_result, tool_error, error, and response_complete messages. A stable application contract lets the UI evolve independently of ADK and supports a future orchestrator adapter.
Why: Map provider or framework events into a versioned public contract. Persist the answer before exposing its final message ID and keep internal tool arguments out of the public stream.
Risk: Forwarding raw runtime objects can leak fields and break the UI after dependency changes. A stream ending at the network layer is not necessarily a successful response_complete event.
Trade: An adapter adds code and preserves product stability. Direct runtime streaming is quicker for a demo and creates tighter coupling.
Try: Capture a synthetic successful and failed stream. Verify event discriminators, JSON validity, and exactly one meaningful terminal outcome for the actual route path.

Q: How should a browser parse streaming chunks correctly?
A: Buffer bytes across network reads, decode incrementally, split complete SSE frames, parse their JSON, and retain any unfinished suffix. A network chunk may contain half a JSON object or several events; it is not an event boundary.
Why: Decode UTF-8 incrementally and accumulate SSE fields through the blank-line delimiter. Validate the completed event payload separately and test every relevant network fragmentation boundary.
Risk: Naive JSON.parse on each read loses events or fails on multibyte characters. Error recovery must also distinguish a malformed event from a clean terminal completion.
Trade: A small parser handles a narrow contract; a mature SSE client can cover more protocol details. Test the actual API framing and reconnection requirements.
Try: Feed the same stream split at every possible byte boundary, including inside Unicode text. Verify identical parsed events.
spoken: Decode bytes incrementally, preserve partial UTF-8 state and parse the transport’s actual event framing before parsing JSON. Track operation identity, sequence/replay, partial content and explicit completion separately. Bound buffers and reject malformed or conflicting events.

follow_ups.Q: Does a fetch chunk correspond to one SSE event?
follow_ups.A: No. Network chunk boundaries are arbitrary. SSE fields and blank-line framing need a compatible parser.

Q: Why do persisted message IDs matter for feedback?
A: Feedback should reference an actual assistant message owned by the user, not a temporary browser-generated ID. The backend can then authorize the record and connect a rating to its conversation, evidence, model configuration, and trace.
Why: Bind feedback to an owner-scoped persisted answer or operation. A client-supplied message ID must not allow another user to label or retrieve private conversation data.
Risk: Rating an optimistic local ID can fail or attach feedback to the wrong turn. A persistence failure may leave partial text visible but no authoritative message to rate.
Trade: Waiting for server identity adds a final synchronization step and preserves referential integrity. Client-only messages are easy to render and weak as durable references.
Try: Simulate a stream that generates text but fails persistence. Define whether feedback is disabled and how retry behaves without duplicating the displayed answer.

Q: What should the UI state machine distinguish during a turn?
A: Distinguish draft, accepted, searching or tooling, generating, completed, failed, cancelled, and disconnected. Track evidence and persistence status separately where needed. A spinner stopping is not proof that the model completed successfully.
Why: Use explicit waiting, running, streaming, review, complete, incomplete, failed, and cancelled states. Transitions should follow typed outcomes rather than the presence of some generated text.
Risk: Treating every closed connection as completion can show truncated service requests as final. Late responses from a prior conversation or signed-out user can also contaminate current state.
Trade: Explicit states add frontend logic and improve recovery. A single loading boolean is compact and cannot represent the important distinctions.
Try: Create a reducer for stream events and test disconnect before completion, tool failure, persistence failure, cancellation, and a late event after tenant or conversation change.

Q: How should request confirmation be presented and protected in the UI?
A: Display the exact prepared fields, identify that no claim is yet submitted, and send the token through the authenticated confirmation route only after the user's action. Disable duplicate controls for usability while retaining server-side race protection.
Why: Present exact parameters, operation identity, expiry, and revision. Disable misleading repeated actions in the UI, but rely on server-side approval validation and transactional idempotency for correctness.
Risk: Corrections can leave old pending tokens valid unless the server supersedes them. The UI must not promise revocation that only exists in prompt text.
Trade: A review screen adds friction and supports consent to material fields. The authoritative check must remain on the server because browsers can retry or be bypassed.
Try: Test double click, refresh, expired token, cancellation race, and correction after preparation. Compare displayed state with the actual submission record.

Q: How should browser caching respond to sign-out, role changes, and archived conversations?
A: Partition cached results by trusted user and relevant resource identity, cancel or ignore obsolete in-flight responses, and clear private state at sign-out. Revalidate permissions for source opening and mutation even if a cached view once allowed access.
Why: Invalidate or partition client caches by authenticated identity and permission revision. Cancel streams and clear private view state on sign-out, while retaining server-side ownership checks on every fetch.
Risk: Reusing query keys across users can show private content without making a new unauthorized request. Hidden or archived messages can also remain in model context unless their lifecycle is mapped deliberately.
Trade: Aggressive invalidation costs network requests and preserves clear session boundaries. Long-lived caches improve responsiveness and need stronger partitioning and freshness rules.
Try: Switch users during a slow stream and verify no old message, source, or confirmation token appears in the new user's interface.

Q: How should citations and tool activity be rendered accessibly and safely?
A: Render untrusted text safely, expose expandable source details by keyboard, use meaningful labels, and avoid announcing every token to assistive technology. Show user-relevant activity without exposing internal prompts, private tool arguments, or raw exception data.
Why: Render model text as text or a sanitized approved subset. Validate links and avoid treating returned HTML or tool output as trusted application markup.
Risk: Raw HTML or unsafe URLs can create XSS, and a busy live region can make streaming unusable. A similarity distance should not be displayed as percent certainty.
Trade: Progressive disclosure reduces overload but must keep verification discoverable. Detailed internal traces belong in authorized operator tools, not the customer screen.
Try: Review a synthetic answer using only the keyboard and a screen reader. Include malicious markup and long source titles in the fixture.

Q: How should client retries preserve operation identity?
A: Reuse one idempotency key for retries of the same logical request, but create a new operation for a genuinely changed request. Record whether the server accepted or completed it. Claim confirmation should rely on its own token and durable state, not a generic chat response cache.
Why: Preserve a durable operation key across retries and distinguish request deduplication from business idempotency. After an uncertain outcome, query status rather than restarting a write blindly.
Risk: Reusing a key with a changed body should fail rather than replay another answer. Retrying a long-running request after a best-effort Redis wait can still duplicate model calls.
Trade: Explicit operation identity requires lifecycle handling and supports predictable retries. Automatically retrying all failures is easy and can repeat expensive work.
Try: Test same key/same body, same key/changed body, new key/same body, and an ambiguous timeout. Document behavior for chat versus confirmation.

Q: How should frontend, API, and agent contracts be tested together?
A: Use a small set of full user journeys plus focused contract tests for events, ownership, persistence IDs, and confirmation effects. Fake providers make UI tests deterministic; separate live-provider tests assess actual model behavior.
Why: Expose a stable API error and outcome schema across frontend and backend. Version incompatible changes and test clients against missing, delayed, duplicate, and unknown event types.
Risk: A mocked stream that always ends successfully cannot reveal cancellation or malformed-event behavior. Live model tests alone are too variable for every UI assertion.
Trade: Layered tests provide fast diagnosis and credible integration coverage. Excessive end-to-end duplication raises cost without necessarily testing new behavior.
Try: Define five journeys: cited answer, corrected preparation, denied foreign claim, failed stream, and post-restart history. State the provider and database realism each needs.

Q: What should the completed portfolio demonstration show?
A: Show one coherent user journey across authentication, evidence retrieval, streaming, source verification, request preparation, confirmation, background indexing, and feedback. Then demonstrate a denial and a recovery case with supporting traces and tests.
Why: Demonstrate identity, evidence, approved effects, cancellation, restart recovery, and quality measurement in one coherent journey. Use synthetic data and show a failure as well as success.
Risk: A polished recording can hide unimplemented handoff, current-only policy scope, or in-memory deployment state. State those limitations and show the effective configuration.
Trade: A narrow reliable application is more persuasive than many unverified agent features. Add remote agents or model adaptation only when the measured problem justifies them.
Try: Prepare a ten-minute demo with architecture, one successful task, one adversarial denial, one crash recovery, and a held-out quality/cost report.
